With almost all of my wealthy clients, they tend to live in organized messes. Like, they're the ones with messy (cluttered) offices/homes, but know exactly where everything is. One thing they all have in common is they live well within their means. These are the clients who bring in at least $1M annually, so the cars and collectibles are a drop in the bucket for them.

All of the super-wealthy clients have worked their way up from nothing. The wealthier ones who came from money don't have nearly as much as/work as hard as those who came from poverty or lived in poverty at some point. The ones who came from money are generally snobbier. All of the super-successful went to college, and either had scholarships or paid out of pocket (including the under 40 clientele). Other than some surgeons, they're all self-employed and philanthropic. They're all fairly right-wing or politically in the middle as well.

The highly successful clients are always extremely driven, and they tell me they see that in me. It's kind of awesome, because I've built a network of highly successful mentors from various disciplines who are always willing to lend some advice or at least just give me the reality of my situation. They've become like an extended family to me.

Several of my contemporaries at college are now worth more than a million (pounds or dollars, take your pick!). This is not particularly surprising, as the academic institutions I attended are generally regarded as among the world's finest, and many of my contemporaries went into the financial industry, working for large investment banks. Their bonuses have generally been enough to make them millionaires. In general, these people tend to be (a) more intelligent than average; (b) harder-working than average; and (c) better able to manage inter-personal relationships than average. I suspect that some of them were also (d) luckier than average, and just happened to be in the right financial market at the right time, but I can't prove this.

More interesting are the two who have become seriously rich so far. By "seriously rich" I mean that their wealth is probably in the mid-tens of millions. One, whom I estimate is probably worth about £20 million, made his money in the entertainment business - he started by organising parties and discos at college, and is now a club/catering/entertainment entrepreneur. What has always set him aside is that he has always wanted to do this, and has followed his ambition with great determination. He was also lucky along the way - he got a chance to to invest in a reasonably well-known UK restaurant chain when it was struggling, and has turned this into a very profitable venture. Did he make his own luck there? I don't know.

The second started an investment company with several colleagues, and this has grown (and continues to grow) as they have increased their funds under management. I estimate his worth to be well north of £50 million. Over the past few years he has made several enormous cash gifts to the college we both attended (seven figure sums each time). He seems to be handling his wealth with appropriate humility, and I haven't heard that he's done much in the way of "conspicuous consumption". Again, his principal personal features are intelligence, hard-work, and a strong drive to follow the path he's set himself.

As for myself, all I can say is that I'm occasionally envious of their wealth and (perhaps) the social status that seems to accrue to the very rich. Do I regret not following the same career path? Perhaps fleetingly, now and then, but most of the time I'm realistic enough to know that my own interests and drives and character don't fit me for an investment bank or a boardroom.
